findings.F1: A coin's 24-hour return, measured in its usual 30-day 24-hour move, is followed by an opposite move over the next 24 hours, and the effect grows with the coin's volatility level. On the 24-hour grid, the slope of the next 24-hour excess return on the past move, both in usual moves, runs from +0.026 (t 1.14) in the lowest volatility quintile through -0.089 (t -4.88) in the middle one to -0.150 (t -8.63) in the highest. Each quintile has about 2,990 independent cases.
findings.F2: In the higher-volatility 40 % of cases, the extreme quintiles reverse by more than a trade costs. After a mean past move of -1.70 usual moves the next 24 hours earn +1.10 % above drift (t 5.15, n 1196). After +1.84 usual moves they earn -0.63 % (t -3.40, n 1196). One trade costs 0.19 %.
findings.F3: Falls reverse more than rises. The graded slope is -0.079 (t -4.18, n 7356) after down days and -0.039 (t -2.56, n 7565) after up days. Over all volatilities, the most negative decile (mean -2.56 usual moves) is followed by +0.83 % excess over 24 hours (t 5.01, n 1495). The most positive decile (+2.75) is followed by -0.34 % (t -2.47).
findings.F4: The 24-hour reversal is persistent rather than one period's luck. The yearly slope is negative in 7 of 8 years, with t at or below -2 in 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2023 and 2025, and near zero or positive only in 2022 (+0.001) and 2024 (+0.038, t 1.58). The coins agree in sign, from BTC at -0.009 (t -0.44) to XMR at -0.075 (t -3.63).
findings.F5: The reversal is not specific to the weekend, against the brief. The graded reversal after Saturday's 24 hours exceeds the other days' by only 0.080 (Welch t 1.48, n 2144 against 12847). The slope at the Sunday 00:00 anchor (-0.115, t -4.81) is close to the one at the Monday anchor (-0.104, t -3.45).
findings.F6: The tested idea's two-day continuation does not show over 48 hours. At the Sunday 00:00 anchor, the directional reversal of the past 48 hours is -0.24 % (t -1.70), and its top quartile is -0.16 % (t -0.50). Over the 48-hour horizon the idea's total move per case is +0.08 %, 0.4 times the cost of one trade.
findings.F7: Coins rise in the hours from 21:00 to 23:00 UTC, more so when the coin is volatile. The hours closing at 21:00 and 22:00 earn +5.45 bp (t 6.75) and +4.36 bp (t 5.66) over the next hour, out of 24 hourly slots. The two hours after the 21:00 close are positive in 7 of 8 years and rise with the coin's hourly-volatility tercile: +4.3 bp (t 3.13), +7.6 bp (t 4.05) and +15.1 bp (t 6.00). Even the top tercile's move stays below the 0.19 % trade cost.
findings.F8: The book's gain is concentrated on Monday. It earns +20.9 bp a day on Mondays while holding the coins earns -1.0 bp; the other weekdays range from -8.3 bp (Sunday) to +1.5 bp. So its little profit comes from the second day of the hold, not from the weekend move it bets on.

ideas.idea: A coin's 24-hour return, measured against its usual 30-day 24-hour move, is followed over the next 24 hours by a move in the opposite direction. The reversal is larger the larger that move and the higher the coin's usual 24-hour move stands against its own longer past.
ideas.consequence: A trader would fade large one-day moves on volatile coins and refuse to fade them in calm stretches.
ideas.name: volatile one-day moves reverse

ideas.idea: A coin's 24-hour fall, measured against its usual 30-day 24-hour move, is followed by a rise over the next 24 hours that is larger the deeper the fall.
ideas.consequence: A trader would buy after deep one-day falls, more the deeper the fall, rather than sell after one-day rallies.
ideas.name: deep daily falls rebound

ideas.idea: A coin's return over the two hours after the 21:00 UTC close is upward, and it is larger the higher the coin's average absolute hourly return over the last 30 days.
ideas.consequence: A trader would time a planned purchase to occur before 21:00 UTC instead of after, especially when the coin is volatile.
ideas.name: late evening UTC drift
